claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous, refined fcc microstructure.
The as-built alloy has an evenly distributed elemental composition.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective oxidation or reduction at grain boundaries.
Selective grain-boundary reactions form brittle intergranular phases.
Localized changes in Al and Cr chemistry weaken cohesion of the fcc matrix.
Loss of cohesion promotes stress concentration and ultimately triggers catastrophic failure.
At elevated temperatures, Al and Cr diffuse to grain boundaries.
In oxidizing gases, grain-boundary enrichment of reactive elements produces brittle intergranular oxides such as alumina or chromia.
In reducing gases, preferential reduction and dealloying produce element-depleted grain-boundary regions.
Intergranular oxides and dealloyed regions compromise grain-boundary cohesion.
Compromised grain-boundary cohesion causes crack initiation and propagation that can result in catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure at 600–800°C will produce continuous or semi-continuous brittle oxide scales along grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure will increase intergranular cracking relative to the as-built state.
Reducing exposure will cause elemental depletion, particularly at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary elemental depletion under reducing conditions will reduce ductility and cause earlier mechanical failure.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to exposures at 600–800°C for durations up to several hundred hours.
At substantially different temperatures or much longer exposure times, other degradation mechanisms may predominate.
